**John Richard Pilger** ([/ˈ p ɪ l dʒ ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); 9 October 1939 – 30 December 2023) was an Australian journalist, writer, scholar and documentary filmmaker.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-1) From 1962, he was based mainly in Britain.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-4) He was also a visiting professor at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") in New York.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-5)

Pilger was a critic of [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_United_States "Foreign policy of the United States"), [Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_Australia "Foreign relations of Australia"), and [British foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_the_United_Kingdom "Foreign relations of the United Kingdom"), which he considered to be driven by an [imperialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperialist "Imperialist") and [colonialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialist "Colonialist") agenda. He criticised his native country's treatment of [Indigenous Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians"). He first drew international attention for his reports on the [Cambodian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_genocide "Cambodian genocide").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-6)

Pilger's career as a documentary filmmaker began with _The Quiet Mutiny_ (1970), made during one of his visits to Vietnam, and continued with over 50 documentaries thereafter. Other works in this form include _[Year Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year\_Zero:\_The\_Silent\_Death\_of\_Cambodia "Year Zero: The Silent Death of Cambodia")_ (1979), about the aftermath of the [Pol Pot regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Rouge "Khmer Rouge") in Cambodia, and _[Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_of\_a\_Nation:\_The\_Timor\_Conspiracy "Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy")_ (1993). His many documentary films on indigenous Australians include _[The Secret Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Secret\_Country:\_The\_First\_Australians\_Fight\_Back "The Secret Country: The First Australians Fight Back")_ (1985) and _[Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia\_(2013\_film) "Utopia (2013 film)")_ (2013). In the British print media, Pilger worked at the _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ from 1963 to 1986,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7) and wrote a regular column for the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ magazine from 1991 to 2014.

Pilger won Britain's Journalist of the Year Award in 1967 and 1979.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-8) His documentaries have gained awards in Britain and abroad,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7) including a [BAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-9) He came fourth in a poll of 50 heroes of all time by the New Statesman in May 2006.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-11)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

John Richard Pilger was born on 9 October 1939[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-13) in [Bondi, New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bondi,_New_South_Wales "Bondi, New South Wales"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7) the son of Claude and Elsie Pilger. His older brother, Graham (1932–2017), was a disabled rights activist who later advised the government of [Gough Whitlam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam "Gough Whitlam").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-GPilger-14) Pilger was of German descent on his father's side,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-15) while his mother had English, German and Irish ancestry; two of his maternal great-great-grandparents were Irish convicts transported to Australia.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-discs-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-18) His mother taught French in school.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-discs-16)

Pilger and his brother attended [Sydney Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Boys_High_School "Sydney Boys High School"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-GPilger-14) where he began a student newspaper, _The Messenger_. He later joined a four-year journalist trainee scheme with the [Australian Consolidated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Consolidated_Press "Australian Consolidated Press").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7)

## Newspaper and television career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Newspaper and television career")]

### Newspaper

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Newspaper")]

Beginning his career in 1958 as a copy boy with the _Sydney Sun_, Pilger later moved to _[Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph\_(Sydney) "The Daily Telegraph (Sydney)")_ in Sydney, where he was a reporter, sportswriter and sub-editor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilgerbio-7)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-19) He also freelanced and worked for the Sydney _Sunday Telegraph_, the daily paper's sister title. After moving to Europe, he was a freelance correspondent in Italy for a year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Hayward4-20)

Settling in London in 1962 and working as a sub-editor, Pilger joined British United Press and then [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters") on its Middle-East desk.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Hayward4-20) In 1963, he was recruited by the English _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_, again as a sub-editor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Hayward4-20) Later, he advanced to become a reporter, a feature writer, and chief foreign correspondent for the title. While living and working in the United States for the _Daily Mirror_, on 5 June 1968 he witnessed the [assassination of Robert F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Robert_F._Kennedy "Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy") in Los Angeles during his presidential campaign.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-21) He was a [war correspondent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_correspondent "War correspondent") in [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_humanitarian_crisis "Cambodian humanitarian crisis"), [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War "Bangladesh Liberation War") and [Biafra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Civil_War "Nigerian Civil War"). Nearly eighteen months after [Robert Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Maxwell "Robert Maxwell") bought the _Mirror_ (on 12 July 1984), Pilger was sacked by [Richard Stott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Stott "Richard Stott"), the newspaper's editor, on 31 December 1985.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-22) Pilger was banned from South Africa in 1967.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-:1-23)

Pilger was a founder of the _[News on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News\_on\_Sunday "News on Sunday")_ tabloid in 1984 and became its editor-in-chief in 1986.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Heroes572-24) During the period of hiring staff, Pilger was away for several months filming _The Secret Country_ in Australia. Prior to this, he had given editor Keith Sutton a list of people who he thought might be recruited for the paper, but found on his return to Britain that none of them had been hired.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-25)

Pilger, however, came into conflict with those around him. He disagreed with the founders' decision to base the paper in Manchester and then clashed with the governing committees; the paper was intended to be a workers' co-operative.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Greenslade494-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-27) Sutton's appointment as editor was Pilger's suggestion, but he fell out with Sutton over his plan to produce a left-wing _[Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sun\_(United\_Kingdom) "The Sun (United Kingdom)")_ newspaper.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Greenslade494-26) The two men ended up producing their own dummies, but the founders and the various committees backed Sutton.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Greenslade494-26) Pilger, appointed with "overall editorial control",[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Heroes572-24) resigned at this point before the first issue appeared.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-28) The first issue appeared on 27 April 1987 and _The News on Sunday_ soon closed.

Pilger returned to the _Mirror_ in 2001 after the [9/11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), while [Piers Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piers_Morgan "Piers Morgan") was editor.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-29) In discussing why he left the paper after only being there for 18 months, he told Ian Burrell of the Independent in 2008: "It was a very rewarding 18 months," he says. "I was happy to keep on writing for the Mirror, but Piers was under pressure from the management and American shareholders who objected to the kind of journalism that he was publishing, often written by me. It was a myth that the readers didn't want a serious approach to journalism in a popular newspaper.""[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-:2-30)

His most frequent outlet for many years was the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_, where he had a fortnightly column from 1991 when [Steve Platt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Platt "Steve Platt") was editor to 2014.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Walker-32) In 2018, Pilger said his "written journalism is no longer welcome" in the mainstream and that "probably its last home" was in _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_. His last column for _The Guardian_ was in November 2019.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Walker-32)

Pilger's work often drew criticism from the political right. _The Guardian_'s obituary noted: "The ferocity of right-wing criticism of his views indicated the effectiveness of his journalism."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-33) The right-wing journalist [Auberon Waugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auberon_Waugh "Auberon Waugh") criticised Pilger's work (Waugh's own ethics with regard to journalism were noted by the Guardian in his obituary: "Once [Waugh] discovered the delights of the "freebie", he gave breathless accounts of his trips to the Orient, and the wonderful "Thai two-girl massage".)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-34) Waugh used the phrase "to Pilger" in reference to John Pilger, intending it to mean "presenting information in a sensationalist manner in support of a particular conclusion".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-The_Telegraph_2023_x6742-35)

In its obituary for Pilger, the _[Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Telegraph "Daily Telegraph")_, wrote that "many regarded Pilger as the finest crusading journalist of his generation. He did much to draw world attention to some of the most notorious human rights abuses of the late 20th century". It criticised his 1990 coverage of the Cambodian genocide for not identifying Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge as communists, and criticised his praise for the Vietnam-backed government of Hun Sen for not mentioning that Hun Sen was a former member of the Khmer Rouge. [Noam Chomsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noam_Chomsky "Noam Chomsky") said that Pilger made people uncomfortable by exposing the awful reality of US foreign policy. The U.K. journalist [William Shawcross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shawcross "William Shawcross") described Pilger as "dangerous to the causes which he claims to espouse".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-The_Telegraph_2023_x6742-35)

### Television

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Television")]

With the actor [David Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Swift_(actor) "David Swift (actor)"), and the film makers [Paul Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Watson_(documentary_filmmaker) "Paul Watson (documentary filmmaker)") and [Charles Denton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Denton_(television_and_film_producer) "Charles Denton (television and film producer)"), Pilger formed Tempest Films in 1969. "We wanted a frontman with a mind of his own, rather like another [James Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cameron_(journalist) "James Cameron (journalist)"), with whom [Richard [Marquand]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Marquand "Richard Marquand") had worked", Swift once said. "Paul thought John was very charismatic, as well as marketing extremely original, refreshingly radical ideas." The company was unable to gain commissions from either the BBC or [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_(TV_channel) "ITV (TV channel)"), but did manage to package potential projects.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-36)

Pilger's career on television began on _[World in Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World\_in\_Action "World in Action")_ ([Granada Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_Television "Granada Television")) in 1969, directed by Denton, for whom he made two documentaries broadcast in 1970 and 1971, the earliest of more than fifty in his career. _The Quiet Mutiny_ (1970) was filmed at Camp Snuffy, presenting a character study of the common US soldier during the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). It revealed the shifting [morale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morale "Morale") and open rebellion of American troops. Pilger later described the film as "something of a scoop" – it was the first documentary to show the problems with morale among the drafted ranks of the US military. In an interview with the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_, Pilger said:

> When I flew to New York and showed it to [Mike Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Wallace "Mike Wallace"), the star reporter of [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS")' _[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60\_Minutes "60 Minutes")_, he agreed. "Real shame we can't show it here".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-37)

He made other documentaries about the United States involvement in Vietnam, including _Vietnam: Still America's War_ (1974), _Do You Remember Vietnam?_ (1978), and _[Vietnam: The Last Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam:\_The\_Last\_Battle "Vietnam: The Last Battle")_ (1995).

During his work with BBC's _Midweek_ television series during 1972–73,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Hayward5-38) Pilger completed five documentary reports, but only two were broadcast.

Pilger was successful in gaining a regular television outlet at [ATV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Television "Associated Television"). The _Pilger_ half-hour documentary series was commissioned by [Charles Denton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Denton_(television_and_film_producer) "Charles Denton (television and film producer)"), then a producer with ATV, for screening on the British ITV network. The series ran for five seasons from 1974 until 1977,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Hayward5-38) at first running in the UK on Sunday afternoons after _[Weekend World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekend\_World "Weekend World")_. The theme song for the series was composed by [Lynsey de Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynsey_de_Paul "Lynsey de Paul").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-39) Later the program was scheduled in a weekday peak-time evening slot. The last series included "A Faraway Country" (September 1977) about dissidents in [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia"), then still part of the Communist Soviet bloc. Pilger and his team interviewed members of [Charter 77](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_77 "Charter 77") and other groups, clandestinely using domestic film equipment. In the documentary Pilger praises the dissidents' courage and commitment to freedom and describes the communist totalitarianism as "fascism disguised as socialism".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-40)

Pilger was later given an hour slot at 9 pm, before _[News at Ten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV\_News\_at\_Ten "ITV News at Ten")_, which gave him a high profile in Britain. After ATV lost its franchise in 1981, he continued to make documentaries for screening on ITV, initially for [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_Central "ITV Central"), and later via [Carlton Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlton_Television "Carlton Television").

## Documentaries and career: 1978–2000

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Documentaries and career: 1978–2000")]

### Cambodia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Cambodia")]

Main article: [Year Zero: The Silent Death of Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Zero:_The_Silent_Death_of_Cambodia "Year Zero: The Silent Death of Cambodia")

In 1979, Pilger and two colleagues with whom he collaborated for many years, documentary filmmaker [David Munro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Munro_(documentary_filmmaker) "David Munro (documentary filmmaker)") and photographer Eric Piper, entered [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia") in the wake of the overthrow of the [Pol Pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Pot "Pol Pot") regime. They made photographs and reports that were world exclusives. The first was published as a special issue of the _[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_, which sold out. They also produced an ITV documentary, _Year Zero: the Silent Death of Cambodia._[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-41) Whilst filming 'Cambodia: Year One" Pilger was placed on a 'death list' by the Khmer Rouge.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-42)

Following the showing of _Year Zero_, some $45 million was raised, unsolicited, in mostly small donations, including almost £4 million raised by schoolchildren in the UK. This funded the first substantial relief to Cambodia, including the shipment of life-saving drugs such as penicillin, and clothing to replace the black uniforms people had been forced to wear. According to Brian Walker, director of [Oxfam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxfam "Oxfam"), "a solidarity and compassion surged across our nation" from the broadcast of _Year Zero_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-43)

[William Shawcross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shawcross "William Shawcross") wrote in his book _The Quality of Mercy: Cambodia, Holocaust and Modern Conscience_ (1984) about Pilger's series of articles about Cambodia in the _Daily Mirror_ during August 1979:

> A rather interesting quality of the articles was their concentration on Nazism and the holocaust. Pilger called Pol Pot 'an Asian Hitler' — and said he was even worse than Hitler . . . Again and again Pilger compared the Khmer Rouge to the Nazis. Their Marxist-Leninist ideology was not even mentioned in the _Mirror_, except to say they were inspired by the Red Guards. Their intellectual origins were described as 'anarchist' rather than Communist".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-West84-44)

[Ben Kiernan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Kiernan "Ben Kiernan"), in his review of Shawcross's book, notes that Pilger did compare Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge to [Stalin's terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Purge "Great Purge"), as well as to [Mao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong")'s [Red Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Guards_(China) "Red Guards (China)"). Kiernan notes instances where other writers' comparisons of Pol Pot to Hitler or the Vietnamese to the Nazis are either accepted by Shawcross in his account, or not mentioned.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Kiernan1984-45)

Shawcross wrote in _The Quality of Mercy_ that "Pilger's reports underwrote almost everything that refugees along the Thai border had been saying about the cruelty of Khmer Rouge rule since 1975, and that had already appeared in the books by the _Reader's Digest_ and François Ponchaud. In _Heroes_, Pilger disputes [François Ponchaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Ponchaud "François Ponchaud") and Shawcross's account of Vietnamese atrocities during [the Vietnamese invasion and near famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_humanitarian_crisis#Vietnamese_invasion_and_famine "Cambodian humanitarian crisis") as being "unsubstantiated".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilger1986-46) Ponchaud had interviewed members of anti-communist groups living in the Thai refugee border camps. According to Pilger, "At the very least the effect of Shawcross's 'exposé'" of Cambodians' treatment at the hands of the Vietnamese "was to blur the difference between Cambodia under Pol Pot and Cambodia liberated by the Vietnamese: in truth, a difference of night and day".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilger1986-46) In his book, Shawcross himself doubted that anyone had died of starvation.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Kiernan1984-45)

Pilger and Munro made four later films about Cambodia. Pilger's documentary _Cambodia – The Betrayal_ (1990), prompted a libel case against him, which was settled at the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Justice "High Court of Justice") with an award against Pilger and Central Television. _The Times_ of 6 July 1991 reported:

> Two men who claimed that a television documentary accused them of being [SAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Air_Service "Special Air Service") members who trained Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge to lay mines, accepted "very substantial" libel damages in the High Court yesterday. Christopher Geidt and Anthony De Normann settled their action against the journalist John Pilger and Central Television on the third day of the hearing. Desmond Browne, QC, for Mr Pilger and Central Television, said his clients had not intended to allege the two men trained the Khmer Rouge to lay mines, but they accepted that was how the program had been understood.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-47)

Pilger said the defence case collapsed because the government issued a gagging order, citing national security, which prevented three government ministers and two former heads of the [SAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Air_Service "Special Air Service") from appearing in court.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-48) The film received a British Academy of Film and Television Award nomination in 1991.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-49)

### Thai slavery story

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Thai slavery story")]

In 1982 Pilger authored an article for the _Daily Mirror_ in which he wrote that he had bought an 8-year-old Thai slave girl for £85, and subsequently to have discovered her village of origin in Northern Thailand and returned her to her mother, with Pilger pledging money to support the girl's education. This story was subsequently cast into doubt by an investigation in the _Far Eastern Economic Review_ (FEER) which uncovered that the girl and her mother had been paid to play their respective parts by a fixer working for Pilger. Pilger accused those involved at FEER of being CIA agents[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. An article by the right-wing journalist [Auberon Waugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auberon_Waugh "Auberon Waugh") to _The Spectator_ cast further doubt on the story. Pilger threatened _The Spectator_ with an action for libel. In responding to [The Bulletin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bulletin_(Australian_periodical) "The Bulletin (Australian periodical)")'s coverage of the issue Pilger wrote the following on 17 August 1982:

**I Do Not Believe I was Hoaxed**

> "I AM sorry The Bulletin published an article about me (August 3) without seeking my side of the story. The writer, Robert Darroch, quoted me but I never spoke to him: a salutary experience for a journalist such as myself. I appreciate the opportunity to make the following facts clear. I am suing The Spectator and its writer, Auberon Waugh, for one reason and one reason only: that in the June 12 issue Waugh gave approval and credibility to a totally untrue and bogus tale from Bangkok that I, together with the author of a United Nations report on child slavery in Thailand, a photographer and a Thai human rights official, somehow “set up” the buying of a child..."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-50)

Pilger went on in his letter to point out that he wasn't in Thailand on the month it was alleged to have occurred.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-51) The matter was settled out of court without any payment to Pilger.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Times_obituary2-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Waugh_19822-53)

### Australia's Indigenous peoples

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Australia's Indigenous peoples")]

Pilger long criticised aspects of Australian government policy, particularly what he regarded as its inherent racism resulting in the poor treatment of [Indigenous Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians"). In 1969, Pilger went with Australian activist [Charlie Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Perkins_(Aboriginal_activist) "Charles Perkins (Aboriginal activist)") on a tour to Jay Creek in Central Australia. He compared what he witnessed in Jay Creek to South African apartheid.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-54) He saw the appalling conditions that the [Aboriginal people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_Australians "Aboriginal Australians") were living under, with children suffering from malnutrition and grieving mothers and grandmothers having had their lighter-skinned children and grandchildren removed by the police and welfare agencies. Equally, he learned of Aboriginal boys being sent to work on white-run farms, and Aboriginal girls working as servants in middle-class homes as undeclared slave labour.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-55)

Pilger made several documentaries about Indigenous Australians, such as _[The Secret Country: The First Australians Fight Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Secret\_Country:\_The\_First\_Australians\_Fight\_Back "The Secret Country: The First Australians Fight Back")_ (1985) and _[Welcome to Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome\_to\_Australia "Welcome to Australia")_ (1999). His book on the subject, _A Secret Country_, was first published in 1989. Pilger wrote in 2000 that the 1998 legislation that removed the common-law rights of Indigenous peoples:

> is just one of the disgraces that has given Australia the distinction of being the only developed country whose government has been condemned as racist by the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-56)

Pilger returned to this subject with _Utopia_, released in 2013 (see below).

### East Timor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: East Timor")]

#### _Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy")]

Main article: [Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_of_a_Nation:_The_Timor_Conspiracy "Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy")

In [East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Timor "East Timor") Pilger clandestinely shot _Death of a Nation: The Timor Conspiracy_ about the brutal [Indonesian occupation of East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesian_invasion_of_East_Timor "Indonesian invasion of East Timor"), which began in 1975.

_Death of a Nation_ contributed to an international outcry which ultimately led to Indonesian withdrawal from [East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Timor "East Timor") and eventual independence in 2000. When _Death of a Nation_ was screened in Britain it was the highest rating documentary in 15 years and 5,000 telephone calls per minute were made to the programme's action line.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-57) When _Death of a Nation_ was screened in Australia in June 1994, Foreign Minister [Gareth Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Evans_(politician) "Gareth Evans (politician)") declared that Pilger "had a track record of distorted [sensationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensationalism "Sensationalism") mixed with sanctimony."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-58)

## Documentaries and career (2000–2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Documentaries and career (2000–2023)")]

### _Palestine Is Still the Issue_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Palestine Is Still the Issue")]

Main article: [Palestine Is Still the Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_Is_Still_the_Issue "Palestine Is Still the Issue")

Pilger's documentary _[Palestine Is Still the Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine\_Is\_Still\_the\_Issue "Palestine Is Still the Issue")_ was released in 2002 and had [Ilan Pappé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilan_Papp%C3%A9 "Ilan Pappé") as historical adviser. Pilger said the film describes how an "historic injustice has been done to the Palestinian people, and until Israel's illegal and brutal occupation ends, there will be no peace for anyone, Israelis included". He said the responses of his interviewees "put the lie to the standard Zionist cry that any criticism of Israel is anti-semitic, a claim that insults all those Jewish people who reject the likes of [Ariel Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Sharon "Ariel Sharon") acting in their name".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Pilger02-59) Its broadcast resulted in complaints by the Israeli embassy, the [Board of Deputies of British Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Deputies_of_British_Jews "Board of Deputies of British Jews"), and the [Conservative Friends of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Friends_of_Israel "Conservative Friends of Israel") that it was inaccurate and biased.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-60)[Michael Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Green_(television_magnate) "Michael Green (television magnate)"), chairman of [Carlton Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlton_Communications "Carlton Communications"), the company that made the film, also objected to it in an interview with _[The Jewish Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Chronicle "The Jewish Chronicle")_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-62)

The UK television regulator, the [Independent Television Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Television_Commission "Independent Television Commission") (ITC), ordered an investigation. The ITC investigation rejected the complaints about the film, stating in its report:

> The ITC raised with Carlton all the significant areas of inaccuracy critics of the programme alleged and the broadcaster answered them by reference to a range of historical texts. The ITC is not a tribunal of fact and is particularly aware of the difficulties of verifying 'historical fact' but the comprehensiveness and authority of Carlton's sources were persuasive, not least because many appeared to be of Israeli origin.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-ITC03-63)

The ITC concluded that in Pilger's documentary "adequate opportunity was given to a pro-Israeli government perspective" and that the programme "was not in breach of the ITC Programme Code".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-ITC03-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Jury-64)

### _Stealing a Nation_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Stealing a Nation")]

Main article: [Stealing a Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealing_a_Nation "Stealing a Nation")

Pilger's documentary _[Stealing a Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealing\_a\_Nation "Stealing a Nation")_ (2004) recounts the [expulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_the_Chagossians "Expulsion of the Chagossians") of the [Chagossians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chagossians "Chagossians") by Britain and the USA between 1967 and 1973 so that the US could construct a military base on their former land. The poor economic situation faced by the Chagossians in [Mauritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauritius "Mauritius") as a result of the deportation is described in the film. After the expulsion, the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") leased [Diego Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Garcia "Diego Garcia"), the largest island in the Chagos Islands, from Britain and constructed a major military base there. In the 21st century, the US used the base for planes which were bombing targets in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In a 2000 ruling on the events, the [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") described the wholesale removal of the Chagossian peoples from the Chagos Islands by Britain as "a [crime against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_against_humanity "Crime against humanity")". Pilger strongly criticised [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") for failing to respond in a substantive way to the 2000 [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Justice "High Court of Justice") ruling that the expulsion of the [Chagossian people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chagossians "Chagossians") to Mauritius was illegal.

In March 2005, _[Stealing a Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealing\_a\_Nation "Stealing a Nation")_ received the [Royal Television Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Television_Society "Royal Television Society") Award.

### Latin America: _The War on Democracy_ (2007)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Latin America: The War on Democracy (2007)")]

Main article: [The War on Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_War_on_Democracy "The War on Democracy")

The documentary _[The War on Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_War\_on\_Democracy "The War on Democracy")_ (2007) was Pilger's first film to be released in the cinema. In "an unremitting assault on American foreign policy since 1945", according to [Andrew Billen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Billen "Andrew Billen") in _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_, the film explores the role of US interventions, overt and covert, in toppling a series of governments in the region, and placing "a succession of favourably disposed bullies in control of its Latino backyard".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-65) It discusses the US role in the [overthrow in 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Chilean_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1973 Chilean coup d'état") of the democratically elected Chilean leader [Salvador Allende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Allende "Salvador Allende"), who was replaced by the military dictatorship of [General Augusto Pinochet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_Pinochet "Augusto Pinochet"). Pilger interviews several ex-[CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA "CIA") agents who purportedly took part in secret campaigns against democratic governments in South America. It also contains what [Peter Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bradshaw "Peter Bradshaw") in _The Guardian_ described as "a dewy-eyed interview" with President [Hugo Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez "Hugo Chávez") of Venezuela, which has moments of "almost _Hello!_-magazine deference".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Bradshaw-66)

Pilger explores the US Army [School of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_the_Americas "School of the Americas") in the US state of Georgia. Generations of South American military were trained there, with a curriculum including [counter-insurgency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-insurgency "Counter-insurgency") techniques. Attendees reportedly included members of Pinochet's security services, along with men from [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti"), [El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador"), [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") and Brazil who have been implicated in human rights abuses.

The film also details the [attempted overthrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Venezuelan_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_attempt "2002 Venezuelan coup d'état attempt") of Venezuela's President [Hugo Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez "Hugo Chávez") in 2002, and the response of the people of [Caracas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracas "Caracas"). It looks at the wider rise of populist governments across South America, led by figures calling for loosening ties with the United States and attempting a more equitable redistribution of the continent's natural wealth. Of "Chávez's decision to bypass the National Assembly for 18 months, and rule by decree", Peter Bradshaw writes "Pilger passes over it very lightly".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Bradshaw-66)

Pilger said the film is about the struggle of people to free themselves from a modern form of slavery. These people, he says,

> describe a world not as American presidents like to see it as useful or expendable, they describe the power of courage and humanity among people with next to nothing. They reclaim noble words like democracy, freedom, liberation, justice, and in doing so they are defending the most basic human rights of all of us in a war being waged against all of us.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-67)

_The War on Democracy_ won the Best Documentary category at the [One World Media Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_World_Media_Awards "One World Media Awards") in 2008.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-68)

### _The War You Don't See_ (2010)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: The War You Don't See (2010)")]

The subject of _The War You Don't See_ is the role of the media in making war. It concentrates on the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories. It begins with the [Collateral Murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collateral_Murder "Collateral Murder") video leaked by [Chelsea Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Manning "Chelsea Manning") and released by [WikiLeaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WikiLeaks "WikiLeaks"). In an interview, Julian Assange describes WikiLeaks as an organisation that gives power to conscientious objectors within power systems. The documentary contends that the media, far from acting as the fourth estate, instead uncritically reports the official line and spin from governments, and thus delivers propaganda rather than journalism. Pilger states that "propaganda relies on us in the media to aim its deceptions not at a far away country but at you at home".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Telegraph12-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-73)

#### Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Reception")]

In its review, _Time Out_ magazine said: "This wonderfully researched and outraged film gathers and presents the case for the prosecution. In a world of embedded reporters, sophisticated spin and governmental evasion, what price investigative journalism?"[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-74)

For Christopher Czechowicz of the [Frontline Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontline_Club "Frontline Club"): "Perhaps what’s most important about this film is its simple message. For John Pilger, the mainstream Fourth Estate is not doing its job properly. Whereas independent journalists are able to articulate the truth in a sophisticated manner, mainstream sources remain disinterested in their work. Time and again, they prefer baseless information, sound bytes and sensational footage of clamoring crowds that rouse emotion to the hard tasks journalists must perform. In Pilger’s final remarks in the film, what remains clear is that more than ever, uncompromised, brave journalism is needed in our world, always challenging the official story, in his words, “however patriotic it appears, or however seductive or insidious it is.”[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-75)

When interviewed about the film on [Al Jazeera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jazeera_English "Al Jazeera English")'s [The Listening Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Listening_Post "The Listening Post") he was asked that the media could in fact prevent war, Pilger replied that in his own view that the media could in fact stop a war from occurring.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-77)

Having been criticised directly in the documentary, with Pilger interviewing [Fran Unsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Unsworth "Fran Unsworth"), the then BBC Head of Newsgathering about its war coverage. The former BBC World News editor, Jon Williams responded to the charge of embedded journalism no longer being objective with the following: "But "embedding" does have real value. There are 9,500 British troops in Afghanistan - and more than 100,000 US service personnel. Theirs is an important perspective, and their operations an important part of the story. The security situation means, sometimes, it is only possible to travel to certain parts of the country as part of a military "embed"."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-78)

[John Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lloyd_(journalist) "John Lloyd (journalist)") in the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_ said _The War You Don't See_ was a "one-sided" documentary which "had no thought of explaining, even hinting, that the wars fought by the US and the UK had a scrap of just cause, nor of examining the nature of what Pilger simply stated were "lies" – especially those that took the two countries to the invasion of Iraq".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Lloyd2010-79)

### _Utopia_ (2013)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Utopia (2013)")]

Main article: [Utopia (2013 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia_(2013_film) "Utopia (2013 film)")

With _Utopia_, Pilger returned to the experiences of Indigenous Australians and what he termed "the denigrating of their humanity".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Macnab-80) A documentary feature film, it takes its title from [Utopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utopia,_Northern_Territory "Utopia, Northern Territory"), an Aboriginal [homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outstation_(Aboriginal_community) "Outstation (Aboriginal community)") (also known as an outstation)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-81) in the [Northern Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Territory "Northern Territory").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-82) Pilger says that "in essence, very little" has changed since the first of his seven films about the Aboriginal people, _A Secret Country: The First Australians_ (1985).[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-83) In an interview with the UK based _Australian Times_ he commented: "the catastrophe imposed on Indigenous Australians is the equivalent of apartheid, and the system has to change".[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-84)

Reviewing the film, [Peter Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bradshaw "Peter Bradshaw") wrote: "The awful truth is that Indigenous communities are on mineral-rich lands that cause mouths to water in mining corporation boardrooms".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-85) "When the subject and subjects are allowed to speak for themselves – when Pilger doesn't stand and preach – the injustices glow like throbbing wounds", wrote [Nigel Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Andrews "Nigel Andrews") in the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_, but the documentary maker "goes on too long. 110 minutes is a hefty time in screen politics, especially when we know the makers' message from scene one".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-86)

Geoffrey Macnab described it as an "angry, impassioned documentary"[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Macnab-80) while for [Mark Kermode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Kermode "Mark Kermode") it is a "searing indictment of the ongoing mistreatment" of the first Australians.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-87)

### _The Coming War on China_ (2016)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: The Coming War on China (2016)")]

_The Coming War on China_ was Pilger's 60th film for ITV.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-88)

The film premiered in the UK on Thursday 1 December 2016,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-89) and was shown on ITV at 10.40 pm on Tuesday 6 December and on the Australian public broadcaster [SBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)") on 16 April 2017.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-90) In the documentary, according to Pilger, "the evidence and witnesses warn that nuclear war is no longer a shadow, but a contingency. The greatest build-up of American-led military forces since the Second World War is well under way. They are on the western borders of Russia, and in Asia and the Pacific, confronting China. Like the renewal of post-Soviet Russia, the rise of China as an economic power is declared an 'existential threat' to the divine right of the United States to rule and dominate human affairs".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-91)

"The first third told, and told well, the unforgivable, unconscionable tale of what has overtaken the Marshall Islanders since 1946, when the US first nuked the test site on Bikini Atoll" beginning an [extended series of tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_testing_at_Bikini_Atoll "Nuclear testing at Bikini Atoll"), wrote Euan Ferguson in _The Observer_. "Over the next 12 years they would unleash a total of 42.2 megatons. The islanders, as forensically proved by Pilger, were effectively guinea pigs for [the] effects of radiation".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Ferguson-92) Ferguson wrote that the rest of the film "was a sane, sober, necessary, deeply troubling bucketful of worries".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-Ferguson-92)[Peter Bradshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bradshaw "Peter Bradshaw") in _The Guardian_ wrote that the film "lays bare the historical horrors of the US military in the Pacific, exposing the paranoia and pre-emptive aggression of its semi-secret bases," adding: "This is a gripping film, which though it comes close to excusing China ... does point out China's insecurities and political cruelties".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-93) Neil Young of _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")_ called the film an "authoritative indictment of American nefariousness in the western Pacific".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-94)

Kevin Maher wrote in _The Times_ that he admired the early sequences on the Marshall Islands, but that he believed the film lacked nuance or subtlety. Maher wrote that, for Pilger, China is "a brilliant place with just some 'issues with human rights', but let's not go into that now".[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-95)_[Diplomat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Diplomat\_(magazine) "The Diplomat (magazine)")_ columnist David Hutt said "Pilger consistently glosses over China's past crimes while dwelling on America's".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-96)

### _The Dirty War on the National Health Service_ (2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: The Dirty War on the National Health Service (2019)")]

Pilger's _The Dirty War on the National Health Service_ was released in the UK on 29 November 2019 and examined the changes that the [NHS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service "National Health Service") had undergone since its founding in 1948. Pilger makes the case that governments beginning with that of Margaret Thatcher have waged a secret war against the NHS with a view to privatising it slowly and surreptitiously. Pilger predicted that moves toward privatisation would create more poverty and homelessness and that the resulting chaos would be used as an argument for further "reform". Prior to the [2019 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), ITV were embargoed from publicising the documentary (as the election was on the 12th of December 2019). It was later broadcast on 17 December 2019.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-97) It was also referenced in a 2020 essay in The Nation magazine, "_How to Destroy a National Health Service_".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-98)

#### Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Reception")]

Peter Bradshaw described the documentary as a "fierce, necessary film".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-99) Emma Simmonds of the Radio Times said: "Pilger is a constant, typically authoritative, slightly doom-laden presence."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-100)

## Views (1999–2023)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Views (1999–2023)")]

### Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Australia")]

Writing for the New Matilda in 2020: "Today, Australia is a vassal state bar none: its politics, intelligence agencies, military and much of its media are integrated into Washington’s “sphere of dominance” and war plans. In Donald Trump's current provocations of China, the US bases in Australia are described as the “tip of the spear”.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-101)

### Bush, Blair, Howard and wars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Bush, Blair, Howard and wars")]

[![Image 5: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **relies excessively on [references](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability") to [primary sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")**. Please improve this section by adding [secondary or tertiary sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")._(August 2022)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

In 2003 and 2004, Pilger criticised United States President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), saying that he had used the [9/11 terrorist attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks") as an excuse to [invade Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq") as part of a strategy to increase US control of the world's oil supplies.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-glw120203-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-103) In 2004, Pilger criticised British Prime Minister [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") as equally responsible for the invasion and the bungled [occupation of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iraq_(2003%E2%80%932011) "History of Iraq (2003–2011)").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-104) In 2004, as the Iraq insurgency increased, Pilger wrote that the anti-war movement should support "Iraq's anti-occupation resistance:

> We cannot afford to be choosy. While we abhor and condemn the continuing loss of innocent life in Iraq, we have no choice now but to support the [resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_insurgency_(2003%E2%80%932011) "Iraqi insurgency (2003–2011)"), for if the resistance fails, the "Bush gang" will attack another country".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-105)

Pilger described Australian Prime Minister [John Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howard "John Howard") as "the mouse that roars for America, whipping his country into war fever and paranoia about terrorism within". He thought Howard's willingness to "join the Bush/Blair assault on Iraq ... evok[ed] a melancholy history of obsequious service to great power: from the [Boxer Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxer_Rebellion "Boxer Rebellion") to the [Boer war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boer_War "Boer War"), to the [disaster at Gallipoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli_campaign "Gallipoli campaign"), and [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"), [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") and the [Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War")".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-106)

On 25 July 2005, Pilger ascribed blame for the [2005 London bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_July_2005_London_bombings "7 July 2005 London bombings") that month to Blair. He wrote that Blair's decision to follow Bush helped to generate the rage that Pilger said precipitated the bombings.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-107)

In his column a year later, Pilger described Blair as a [war criminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_criminal "War criminal") for supporting Israel's actions during the [2006 Israel–Lebanon conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Lebanon_War "2006 Lebanon War"). He said that Blair gave permission to Israeli Prime Minister [Ariel Sharon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Sharon "Ariel Sharon") in 2001 to initiate what would ultimately become [Operation Defensive Shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Defensive_Shield "Operation Defensive Shield").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-108)

In 2014, Pilger wrote that "The truth about the criminal bloodbath in Iraq cannot be "countered" indefinitely. Neither can the truth about our support for the medievalists in [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), the nuclear-armed predators in Israel, the new military fascists in [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and the jihadist "liberators" of Syria, whose propaganda is now BBC news".[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-109)

### Barack Obama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Barack Obama")]

Pilger criticised [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") during his presidential campaign of 2008, saying that he was "a glossy [Uncle Tom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Tom "Uncle Tom") who would bomb [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")"[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-110) and his theme "was the renewal of America as a dominant, avaricious bully". After Obama was elected and took office in 2009, Pilger wrote, "In his first 100 days, Obama has excused torture, opposed _[habeas corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas\_corpus "Habeas corpus")_ and demanded more secret government".[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-111)

[Sunny Hundal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Hundal "Sunny Hundal") wrote in _The Guardian_ during November 2008 that the "Uncle Tom" comment used against Obama "highlights a patronising attitude towards ethnic minorities. Pilger expects all black and brown people to be revolutionary brothers and sisters, and if they veer away from that stereotype, it can only be because they are pawns of a wider conspiracy".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-112)

### Capitalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Capitalism")]

Pilger was [opposed to capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-capitalism "Anti-capitalism"), believing it to be an unjust system.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Pilger#cite_note-anderson93-114)

### Support for Julian Assange

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Pilger&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Support for Julian Assange")]
